source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency for Efficient Reasoning and Coding with LLMs
finding: A direct bounded-accumulation stopper for LLM answers. After each sample, compute the chance the current top answer stays the majority. Stop when it passes a threshold.
numbers: 17 datasets, 3 models (GPT-3.5-turbo, Vicuna-13B, code-davinci-002). Threshold 0.95. Average sample budget cut 3.3x with 0.04% accuracy drop. Up to 7.9x on Boolean Expressions with no loss. Under 5 samples on average on SVAMP.
limits: Needs i.i.d. samples. Paper says it is expected to fail where self-consistency fails.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM analogue of a drift-diffusion bound: the vote lead is the decision variable, the threshold is the bound. Usable as the stopping rule for the number of attempts.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency for Efficient Reasoning and Coding with LLMs
finding: Six stopping rules compared: random, majority, entropy, Beta, Dirichlet, Chinese Restaurant Process. The Beta rule (top two answers only) matches the full Dirichlet and CRP versions but runs about four orders of magnitude faster.
numbers: Beta uses Beta(v1+1,v2+1). Stopping-rule time about 0.03 ms vs about 95-101 ms for Dirichlet/CRP. Random stopping worst; majority-only mostly worse than Beta and entropy at equal cost.
limits: Cost of the stop rule is negligible next to LLM calls either way.
agent_relevance: Only the lead of first over second answer matters. A two-count rule is enough and takes a few lines of code.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency for Efficient Reasoning and Coding with LLMs
finding: At equal average sample cost the adaptive rule beats fixed-N voting, most at low budgets. Accuracy rises with threshold then plateaus while cost climbs steeply.
numbers: GSM-8K: at average cost 10 samples, about 3% higher accuracy than fixed self-consistency. Three seeds, two-sample t-test: generation count p about 1.5e-3 on average, accuracy difference not significant.
limits: Threshold tuned on GSM-8K train then reused across all datasets.
agent_relevance: Past the plateau, more attempts buy little; the knee of this curve is the bound to pick.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning in language models
finding: The fixed-N baseline every later stopper is measured against: sample many reasoning paths, take the most frequent final answer.
numbers: 40 samples per run, averaged over 10 runs. Gains over greedy chain of thought: GSM8K +17.9%, SVAMP +11.0%, AQuA +12.2%. Gains grew with model scale: +3-6% on UL2-20B but +9-23% on LaMDA-137B and GPT-3.
limits: Fixed budget; no stopping rule. Cost is linear in N.
agent_relevance: Shows the accumulation curve exists: accuracy rises then flattens with N, which is what makes a bound sensible.

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape Sky-High Cost: Early-Stopping Self-Consistency for Multi-Step Reasoning
finding: Window rule: draw samples in small windows; stop the first time all answers in a window agree (zero entropy). No threshold to tune.
numbers: Sample reductions vs self-consistency: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%. Window 8 for MATH (max 64), 5 for others (max 40). GPT-4, GPT-3.5-Turbo, Llama-2 7B.
limits: Unanimity in a window can be a confident wrong answer. Reported accuracy changes all within about 0.2 points of self-consistency.
agent_relevance: A cheap unanimity bound: stop when a short run of attempts all agree.

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape Sky-High Cost: Early-Stopping Self-Consistency for Multi-Step Reasoning
finding: Per-model detail: average samples used is far below the max while accuracy is almost unchanged. Giving plain self-consistency the same reduced N loses more accuracy.
numbers: GPT-4 GSM8K: 7.98 samples vs 40, accuracy 89.29 vs 89.29. GPT-3.5 GSM8K: 14.65 samples, 85.69 -> 85.67; self-consistency at the same N: 84.82. GPT-4 MATH: 42.4 of 64 samples, 60.32 unchanged. Llama-2 7B MATH: 62.48 of 64 samples, accuracy 7.68 unchanged.
limits: Weak models on hard tasks save almost nothing.
agent_relevance: Hard problems keep the sampler running: the bound self-adjusts to difficulty, as a diffusion model with low drift rate takes longer.

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape Sky-High Cost: Early-Stopping Self-Consistency for Multi-Step Reasoning
finding: A control scheme predicts cost and accuracy from only the first window, so budget and window size can be chosen in advance. Also works on open-ended code (MBPP) with text-similarity voting.
numbers: Predicted vs actual samples and performance change correlated, p<0.05 (L1 norm and Pearson). Robust to window size, top-p, zero-shot and demonstration choice.
limits: Authors argue Adaptive-Consistency needs extra data to tune its threshold and is threshold-sensitive, and needs one call per sample (the prompt is re-sent each time).
agent_relevance: Windowed batches cut latency in a real agent: run 3 to 5 attempts in parallel, check agreement, then decide.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Make Every Penny Count: Difficulty-Adaptive Self-Consistency for Cost-Efficient Reasoning
finding: Adds a prior on question difficulty to the stopping rule: rank questions by difficulty first, give easy ones a small pre-allocated budget, then use a posterior stopping rule.
numbers: Cost cut vs self-consistency: GPT-4 -65.29% on average, GPT-3.5-Turbo -56.04%. Against the strongest baseline (ESC): -24.81% (GPT-4), -21.86% (GPT-3.5). Six benchmarks, accuracy about equal.
limits: Needs a difficulty-ranking pass that itself costs tokens.
agent_relevance: A prior before the first attempt (like a starting point bias in a diffusion model) lowers cost beyond a pure posterior rule.

source: Wan et al. (2025) Reasoning-Aware Self-Consistency: Leveraging Reasoning Paths for Efficient LLM Sampling
finding: Scores each sample's reasoning and answer, stops once enough high-quality samples are gathered, and weights votes by that quality.
numbers: About 70% fewer samples at similar accuracy; about 80% less inference time than self-consistency. Harder subject (Abstract Algebra) needed 8.54 samples vs 6.15 for College Math.
limits: Feature extraction is the largest non-inference time cost; the quality scorer must be reliable.
agent_relevance: Evidence can be weighted by sample quality, like weighting an evidence increment by its reliability.

source: Taubenfeld et al. (2025) Confidence Improves Self-Consistency in LLMs (CISC)
finding: Votes weighted by each path's own confidence reach the same accuracy with fewer samples. Best confidence signal was P(True), asking the model whether its own answer is correct.
numbers: 9 LLMs, 4 datasets. P(True) cuts cost 41% at budget 5 and 46% at budget 10; some settings over 67%. Self-consistency needs 18.6 samples to match CISC at 10. Gemma2-9B on MATH: CISC at 8 samples beats 30-sample self-consistency (73% cost cut).
limits: Confidence must be normalised within each question (softmax, tuned temperature); gain shrinks without it.
agent_relevance: Confidence is a usable per-attempt evidence weight. Guardrail G5 still applies: self-grading can be biased, so code normalises and an external check is preferred.

source: Taubenfeld et al. (2025) Confidence Improves Self-Consistency in LLMs (CISC)
finding: The best calibrated confidence method was the least useful for CISC. What matters is telling right from wrong answers to the same question, not across questions. The authors define Within-Question Discrimination (WQD) and show it predicts CISC gains.
numbers: Between-question metrics (ECE, Brier) were poor predictors of CISC gain; WQD predicted which method gave the best cost reduction (Table 3).
limits: Single study; a metric defined by the authors.
agent_relevance: If attempts are weighted by confidence, evaluate the signal within a problem, not across problems.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Uses token-level confidence inside each reasoning trace: drop low-confidence traces early (online) or filter and weight votes (offline). A trace halts when running group confidence falls under a threshold set from warm-up traces.
numbers: Offline, 512 traces: GPT-OSS-120B on AIME 2025 99.9% vs 97.0% majority vote vs 91.8% single pass. DeepSeek-8B AIME25 82.3 -> 87.4; Qwen3-32B AIME24 85.3 -> 90.8. Online: tokens cut up to 84.7%.
limits: Models can be confident and wrong; authors name this the key limitation. Online low-threshold variant lost accuracy in a few settings (Qwen3-32B BRUMO25 -0.9).
agent_relevance: A per-trace bound: abandon an attempt when its internal confidence drifts below a floor, so the attempt budget is not wasted on doomed chains.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Two operating points: aggressive (keep top 10% of warm-up confidence) and conservative (keep top 90%). The conservative setting trades savings for safety.
numbers: Aggressive: 43-79% token cut across AIME24/25, BRUMO25, HMMT25; DeepSeek-8B AIME24 +5.8%. Conservative: 18-59% savings at near-identical accuracy.
limits: Warm-up traces cost tokens and set the threshold per problem; no error-rate guarantee.
agent_relevance: Two named bound settings: tight = fast and riskier; wide = slower and safer.

source: Lee et al. (2025) ConSol: Sequential Probability Ratio Testing to Find Consistent LLM Reasoning Paths Efficiently
finding: Applies Wald's sequential probability ratio test (SPRT) and a mixture SPRT directly to repeated answers from reasoning models. Test whether the top answer's share exceeds 0.5 and stop when the likelihood ratio crosses a bound.
numbers: Token reduction up to 84.8% (AIME24, o3-mini-medium) and 86.2% (GPQA Diamond, o3-mini-low). AIME24 o3-mini-low accuracy rose 70.0% to 80.0% vs self-consistency@40 because it may sample past 40 on uncertain items.
limits: Standard SPRT error rates (0.05, 0.10) needed too many samples, so authors re-tuned parameters (p0/p1 nearer 0.5) and the Beta prior; formal type I/II guarantees no longer strictly hold. Models: o3-mini, GPT-4o-mini.
agent_relevance: Most literal match to Wald and Ratcliff: error-rate-controlled sequential test. Also shows the bound should allow going beyond a fixed N on hard items.

source: Lee et al. (2025) ConSol: Sequential Probability Ratio Testing to Find Consistent LLM Reasoning Paths Efficiently
finding: For reasoning models one answer usually dominates (top-answer share p1 above 0.5 in most items); below 0.5 neither of the top two answers is likely correct. This justifies a two-hypothesis test.
numbers: Figures 1-2 show p1 mostly above 0.5 for o3-mini; stronger models more peaked. Simulation: reaches the same consistency with fewer samples than self-consistency and Adaptive-Consistency.
limits: Based on o3-mini family; peakedness differs by model.
agent_relevance: If the top share stays near or under 0.5 after many attempts, treat it as an impasse signal rather than keep sampling.

source: Wang et al. (2025) OptPO: Optimal Rollout Allocation for Test-time Policy Optimization
finding: Bayesian SPRT as the vote counter inside test-time reinforcement learning. Halt rollouts once posterior confidence in the consensus passes a bound; keep retained rollouts as training signal.
numbers: 30-50% fewer tokens on average than TTRL at equal or better mean@16 and pass@16; with N=16 rollouts 43.9% tokens saved, with N=32 30.0%.
limits: Pseudo-labels from consensus can be wrong; this is training, not a pure inference agent.
agent_relevance: Same SPRT idea inside a learning loop; saved compute can go to harder items under a global budget.

source: Liu and Wang (2025) Answer Convergence as a Signal for Early Stopping in Reasoning
finding: Within one long chain of thought, models reach their final answer after about 60% of the steps. Early stop when the answer is unchanged across k consecutive chunks.
numbers: 5 benchmarks, 5 open-weight LLMs. Models converge after about 60% of reasoning on math. NaturalQuestions: over 40% fewer tokens with higher accuracy. k=10 consecutive chunks; boosting end-of-thinking weight 0.6.
limits: Probe cost; savings inconsistent across datasets (one configuration shows +6.3% tokens).
agent_relevance: A within-attempt stopping rule: probe the current answer mid-trace; stop thinking when it has been stable for k probes.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models (DEER)
finding: At reasoning transition points, force a trial answer and exit if the model's confidence in it is high. No training.
numbers: 11 reasoning models (1.5B-671B), 10 benchmarks. Chain length cut 19.1% to 80.1% while accuracy rose 0.3% to 5.0%. Latency -27.9% in one setup. Prompt-based token budgets worked on GSM8K but failed on AIME24, where models ignored length limits.
limits: Needs transition-point detection and a confidence read; gains vary by model.
agent_relevance: Evidence that stopping thinking early can raise accuracy: extra thinking past the bound adds overthinking error. Prompted limits are not reliable; code must enforce them.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Budget forcing sets both a bound and a floor: cut thinking at a maximum token count, or suppress the end token and append Wait to force more thinking. A hard external threshold on sequential accumulation.
numbers: s1-32B trained on 1,000 samples. AIME24 rose from 50% to 57% when forced to continue (2, 4, 6 Wait appends). Exceeds o1-preview by up to 27% on MATH and AIME24. Parallel majority voting over up to 64 samples compared in Fig 4(b).
limits: Gains flatten at longer forced budgets; result is for a fine-tuned model.
agent_relevance: Floor and ceiling on attempts: a minimum number of tries before stopping and a hard maximum.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Sampling-Efficient Test-Time Scaling: Self-Estimating the Best-of-N Sampling in Early Decoding (ST-BoN)
finding: Prunes parallel samples early using consistency of their internal states, then finishes only the most promising one. No reward model.
numbers: Same performance as full Best-of-N at 70-80% less cost; GPU memory down over 80%, latency down 50%; at equal cost 3-4 points higher accuracy.
limits: Authors' own benchmarks; relies on early consistency being informative.
agent_relevance: Stop weak attempts early; spend the saved budget on promising ones.

source: Na et al. (2025) Thinker-DDM: Modeling Deliberation for Machine Translation with a Drift-Diffusion Process
finding: An explicit drift-diffusion process inside an LLM pipeline. Start value is a prior preference for one translation system; each new candidate adds evidence scored by CometKiwi; boundaries shrink exponentially so decisions get faster over time.
numbers: WMT22 and CommonMT; outperforms baselines in high- and low-resource translation, but not in commonsense translation by default (a COMET swap was needed for a large gain).
limits: Evidence is scored by another model, not ground truth; boundary decay is a design choice.
agent_relevance: Template for a literal diffusion controller: bias, evidence increments, collapsing bounds. A collapsing bound gives urgency when time runs out.

source: Arthur (2026) Thinking effort aligns between humans and reasoning models in abductive reasoning
finding: Reasoning-token count tracks human reaction time per item on a task with no formal difficulty cues. Humans: N=120 (after exclusions), 160 items, forced choice between two hypotheses.
numbers: Partial r with log human RT (greedy): GPT-OSS-120B 0.552, GPT-OSS-20B 0.41, Qwen3-235B 0.359, DeepSeek-R1 0.327, Kimi-K2 0.303, GLM-4.5-Air 0.263, Qwen3-32B 0.229, non-reasoning DeepSeek-V3 0.197. Model-human item accuracy r=0.668; human accuracy 48.7% when 75%+ of models failed vs 84.6% when 75%+ got it right.
limits: Single task family; token counts are not true time; greedy runs are single trajectories.
agent_relevance: Items that cost humans more time also cost the model more thinking, so effort is a usable difficulty signal for choosing how many attempts to allow.

source: Arthur (2026) Thinking effort aligns between humans and reasoning models in abductive reasoning
finding: Averaging over sampled runs raises alignment with human time: the mean over many trajectories is closer to a human decision time than one greedy path.
numbers: GPT-OSS-20B r 0.41 -> 0.55 (T=1, K=25, Steiger-Williams p<.001); Qwen3-32B 0.23 -> 0.32 (T=0.6, p<.05); R1 0.32 -> 0.37 (not significant). Stable at about 19, 18 and 8 runs. At T=2 alignment fell (GPT-OSS-20B to 0.22).
limits: Pooled estimate converges at roughly 8 to 19 runs.
agent_relevance: About 8 to 19 samples gave a stable mean effort estimate; a useful order of magnitude for a sampling budget.

source: Vats (2026) Good Judgment, Bad Advice: Decision-Model Controllers Raise Agent Cost Without Improving Success
finding: A failed case of delegating the stop decision in an agent loop. A learned controller deciding when to finish or verify raised cost without raising pass rate.
numbers: Terminal-Bench 2.1, 21 held-out tasks, 315 trials, Claude Sonnet 5.5 agent. Cost per attempt x1.19 (95% CI 1.02-1.36); pass rate 73.0% vs 73.0%. Finish ranking AUROC 0.78 (rules 0.62, small LLM 0.60) but miscalibrated: mean P(done)=0.50 when 87% of such runs passed. No controller ever chose to abandon.
limits: Small preprint, one benchmark.
agent_relevance: A good ranking of stop moments did not become a good stop rule. The stop rule must be calibrated; rank quality is not enough. Supports code-checked stops with a simple bound.

source: Wald (1945) Sequential tests of statistical hypotheses; Ratcliff (1978); Gold and Shadlen (2007) - as described in the ConSol appendix
finding: Foundations that the LLM stoppers borrow. The SPRT minimises the average sample number for given error rates when samples are independent and identically distributed. Known from ConSol's description; originals not opened this session.
numbers: Not read directly.
limits: i.i.d. assumption: LLM samples from one model are correlated (our guardrail G4), so error guarantees do not hold exactly.
agent_relevance: The i.i.d. condition is exactly where LLM attempts depart: common-mode errors make a stop on agreement overconfident.

source: Synthesis across Adaptive-Consistency, ESC, DSC, ConSol, DeepConf, CISC
finding: Across these studies, stopping on agreement cuts samples by 2x to 8x with accuracy changes within about 1 point. No study tested the rules where the wrong answer is a consistent shared error.
numbers: Reported reductions range from 33.8% (MATH, ESC) to 86.2% (GPQA tokens, ConSol); 3.3x average (Adaptive-Consistency).
limits: My synthesis of papers read, not a single measurement. All benchmarks have a checkable single answer; accuracy loss is measured against the benchmark label.
agent_relevance: A stop-on-agreement rule is safe for savings on easy items but needs an external check (G3) on hard ones where agreement can be correlated error.

source: Synthesis: where the bound failed or was weak
finding: Boundary conditions found: (1) hard tasks keep sampling near the max (Llama-2 7B on MATH used 62.48 of 64); (2) high-confidence wrong paths (DeepConf limitation); (3) learned stop controllers miscalibrated (Vats 2026); (4) standard SPRT error settings impractical for LLM use (ConSol).
numbers: See lines c06, c12, c14, c24.
limits: Synthesis across papers, not one experiment.
agent_relevance: Treat any stop rule as needing its own calibration check on our tasks before trusting it.
